cards.title: Introduction to Validation
cards.content:
Validation in ASP.NET Core ensures that data submitted by clients meets the business rules and constraints defined by the application before it is processed or stored.

It protects your database from corrupt data and provides meaningful feedback to users.

cards.title: Data Annotations
cards.content:
Data Annotations are attributes in the System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations namespace used to decorate model properties.

public class UserModel {
    [Required]
    [StringLength(100, MinimumLength = 3)]
    public string Username { get; set; }

    [EmailAddress]
    public string Email { get; set; }
}

options.text: To style the HTML output of a form.
To enforce validation rules on model properties.
To encrypt sensitive property values in the database.
To map C# properties to SQL Server columns.

cards.title: ModelState Validation
cards.content: In a Controller action, you can check if incoming data is valid by inspecting the [BLANK] property.

Limits min and max length of strings

cards.title: Custom Validation Attributes
cards.content:
When built-in attributes are not enough, you can create custom validation logic by inheriting from ValidationAttribute.

public class AllowedDomainAttribute : ValidationAttribute {
    private readonly string _domain;
    public AllowedDomainAttribute(string domain) => _domain = domain;
    protected override ValidationResult IsValid(object value, ValidationContext validationContext) {
        // Custom logic here
        return ValidationResult.Success;
    }
}

steps: Client submits HTTP request with payload
Model binding populates C# model from request data
Data annotations and custom validation attributes execute
ModelState.IsValid is evaluated in the Controller action
Action executes or returns BadRequest with errors

cards.title: Introduction to FluentValidation
cards.content:
FluentValidation is a popular third-party library that uses a fluent interface and lambda expressions for building strongly-typed validation rules.

public class UserValidator : AbstractValidator<UserModel> {
    public UserValidator() {
        RuleFor(x => x.Email).NotEmpty().EmailAddress();
    }
}

options.text: It keeps validation rules separate from model classes, adhering to the Single Responsibility Principle.
It replaces Entity Framework Core entirely.
It runs exclusively on the client browser.

cards.title: Client-Side Validation
cards.content:
ASP.NET Core integrates seamlessly with jQuery Validation to provide client-side validation out of the box in MVC and Razor Pages.

By including scripts like jquery.validate.js and jquery.validate.unobtrusive.js, validation happens in the browser before a round-trip to the server occurs, improving user experience.

cards.title: Validation Summary
cards.content:
You have learned about:

  • Using built-in Data Annotations ([Required], [Range], etc.)
  • Checking ModelState.IsValid in controllers
  • Creating custom validation attributes
  • Using FluentValidation for clean separation of concerns
  • Enabling client-side validation for better performance and UX
